sections.domain: Sharing the Road with Trucks, Trailers, Buses and Motorcycles
sections.heading: C — Sharing the Road with Trucks, Trailers, Buses and Motorcycles
sections.markdown:
## C — Sharing the Road with Trucks, Trailers, Buses and Motorcycles

FACT_ID: sec16-F01 | anchor: A01
Trucks, tractor-semitrailers, truck trailers and buses need special skill, attentiveness and consideration to operate, and for everyone's safety other road users must also understand the limitations of these large vehicles [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec16-F02 | anchor: A01
A driver of a large vehicle must hold a valid license for that vehicle category, and because most such drivers drive for a living they should be the most skilled and experienced drivers on the road, setting the example of safe driving while being exposed to driving hazards far longer than ordinary drivers [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec16-F03 | anchor: A01
Because of their size and weight, large vehicles cause great damage and injury in a crash, so their drivers must stay constantly aware of the limits and potential of their vehicles and give proper consideration to other road users, passengers and cargo [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec16-F04 | anchor: A01
A large vehicle's high driving position gives better forward visibility, but visibility to the sides and rear is severely limited, other traffic is seen only through mirrors, and the area immediately behind the vehicle cannot be seen at all [A01].
Why it matters: the blind zone directly behind a truck is the fact most often tested from this page.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec16-F05 | anchor: A01
Drivers of large vehicles must allow for their greater width and length when turning, changing lanes or backing [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec16-F06 | anchor: A02
Other drivers should give a large vehicle extra space for its maneuvers, and when near one should stay where its driver can see them and where their own view of traffic is not blocked, because large vehicles need more room to turn [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec16-F07 | anchor: A02
Large vehicles need greater stopping distances, so their drivers allow for it and other drivers must allow for it too when changing lanes in front of them or at intersections [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec16-F08 | anchor: A02
Large vehicles accelerate very slowly and cannot maneuver as quickly as other vehicles, and they may travel below the posted limit, so use caution when approaching or passing them [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec16-F09 | anchor: A02
Continuous braking to control speed on a downgrade makes brakes ineffective, which is more dangerous for large vehicles, so their drivers shift to a lower gear before a steep descent and other drivers should stay alert for overtaking large vehicles and move out of their way [A02].
Why it matters: a heavy vehicle coming down a grade may be unable to slow, so smaller vehicles clear the path.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec16-F10 | anchor: A02
Large fast-moving vehicles create wind gusts strong enough to push a smaller vehicle off its line, so drivers of smaller vehicles should be ready to correct their steering when approaching or passing large vehicles near top speed [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec16-F11 | anchor: A02
Large trucks often carry explosive, flammable, radioactive, poisonous or other dangerous materials, and their drivers must see that the cargo is packaged and labeled correctly and that the truck itself carries markings showing the type of material, so responders can take the right protective action after a crash [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec16-F12 | anchor: A03
Most large vehicles must carry emergency equipment such as fire extinguishers, flares, emergency reflectors and first aid kits, and their drivers must know what is required and how and when to use it [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec16-F13 | anchor: A03
Many car and small truck drivers tow trailers, and many of the limitations of large vehicles apply to a vehicle towing a trailer, especially a large one [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec16-F14 | anchor: A03
If a trailer is large enough to block the view through the inside rear-view mirror, the towing car must have outside mirrors of proper size on both sides [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec16-F15 | anchor: A03
A loaded trailer that weighs more than half the weight of the towing vehicle, or three thousand pounds or more, must have its own brakes and breakaway protection [A03].
Why it matters: half the tow vehicle's weight or three thousand pounds, whichever comes first, triggers the brake requirement.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec16-F16 | anchor: A03
Passengers should not ride in trailers, and riding in a house trailer is prohibited [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec16-F17 | anchor: A03
A trailer must have safety chains attached to the frame of the towing vehicle and to the trailer, never to a part of the hitch [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec16-F18 | anchor: A04
The towing vehicle needs a hitch proper for the size and type of trailer, large trailers need special hitches, and a bumper hitch should never be relied on for any trailer [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec16-F19 | anchor: A04
A trailer load must be balanced so that about ten to fifteen percent of the trailer's weight rests on the hitch, because too much hitch weight makes steering difficult and too little makes the trailer fishtail, and the trailer must never be overloaded [A04].
Why it matters: ten to fifteen percent on the hitch is the balance rule, and too little causes fishtailing.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0088]

sections.domain: Sharing the Road with Trucks, Trailers, Buses and Motorcycles
sections.heading: C — Sharing the Road with Trucks, Trailers, Buses and Motorcycles (continued)
sections.markdown:
## C — Sharing the Road with Trucks, Trailers, Buses and Motorcycles (continued)

FACT_ID: sec16-F20 | anchor: A04
The load must be held securely in place, and the trailer must have properly mounted and lubricated wheels covered by fenders or mud guards, good properly inflated tires, and tail, stop, turn signal and license plate lamps plus side marker lamps and reflectors where required [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec16-F21 | anchor: A05
Motorcycle riders are friends, relatives and neighbors, motorcycles are fuel and space efficient, but riders are more vulnerable to injury in a crash, and research shows that over two-thirds of car and motorcycle crashes result from a car driver turning in front of the motorcyclist [A05].
Why it matters: the two-thirds figure identifies the car driver's left turn as the main danger.
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec16-F22 | anchor: A06
A motorcycle's narrow silhouette and short length can make it seem farther away and slower than it really is, so a car driver should take a second and a third look, because the small size also makes it harder to spot and some riders cut between cars into places where drivers cannot see them [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec16-F23 | anchor: A06
Before starting a turn or entering an intersection, confirm that you have actually seen any motorcycle and judged its speed [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec16-F24 | anchor: A07
A motorcyclist's position in the lane changes with conditions, often riding in the left portion of the lane to see better and be more visible, but moving to the center or the right side to avoid traffic or be seen [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec16-F25 | anchor: A07
Minor hazards such as potholes or railroad tracks that a car ignores can be major problems for a motorcycle, so the rider shifts position within the lane to gain distance from them, sometimes suddenly, and motorists must be alert for those quick changes [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec16-F26 | anchor: A07
Respect a motorcycle's space and position, because motorcycles are allowed the full width of a lane to maneuver, and never share a lane with a motorcyclist, since that restricts the rider's ability to avoid hazards [A07].
Source: [A07 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec16-F27 | anchor: A08
Intersections are the most likely places for car and motorcycle collisions, usually because the car driver does not see the motorcycle and turns into its path [A08].
Source: [A08 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec16-F28 | anchor: A08
A rider moves to one side of the lane to prepare for a turn or to avoid an unseen hazard, so never assume the rider's intention until the maneuver is unmistakably started, and remember that motorcycle turn signals do not cancel automatically and riders sometimes forget to switch them off [A08].
Why it matters: a blinking motorcycle signal may be a forgotten one, so wait for the actual turn.
Source: [A08 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec16-F29 | anchor: A09
Allow at least a two-second following distance behind a motorcycle so the rider has room to maneuver or stop, and increase the gap further because a motorcycle's speed and distance are hard to judge and sudden braking must be avoided [A09].
Source: [A09 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec16-F30 | anchor: A09
Riders and drivers both make more wrong decisions when stopping distance or the ability to see and react is short, and a rider's injury risk rises when forced to avoid obstacles ahead or when a driver follows too closely [A09].
Source: [A09 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec16-F31 | anchor: A10
Passing rules are similar for motorcycles, so a motorist being overtaken by a motorcycle keeps lane position and speed and lets the rider complete the pass and settle into proper lane position quickly [A10].
Source: [A10 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec16-F32 | anchor: A10
When passing a motorcycle give it a full lane, never crowd into its lane, and do not return to the original lane too soon, because that can force the rider to swerve right into traffic or off the road [A10].
Source: [A10 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec16-F33 | anchor: A10
Motorcycles need special knowledge and skill, so most states require a separate motorcycle knowledge test and skill test for a motorcycle license, and motorcycles must be registered and insured to the same standards as a car [A10].
Source: [A10 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec16-F34 | anchor: A10
Motorcycles are full partners in the traffic mix to be treated with respect and courtesy, so watch for the unexpected and give riders their share of the road [A10].
Source: [A10 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0094]

Misconceptions: the space directly behind a large truck is invisible to its driver, not just hard to see; a motorcycle looks farther away and slower than it is, so a second and third look are needed; a motorcycle's blinking signal may simply be one the rider forgot to cancel; a motorcyclist is entitled to the whole lane, so a car never shares it; the trailer brake rule triggers at half the tow vehicle's weight or at three thousand pounds, whichever applies; too little hitch weight, not too much, causes fishtailing.

Mnemonics: Second look, third look for a motorcycle; two seconds behind it and a full lane beside it; ten to fifteen percent on the hitch, chains to the frame, brakes at three thousand pounds or half the tow weight.

Glossary: tractor-semitrailer (a truck tractor pulling a semitrailer); slipstream (the wind gust a large fast vehicle creates); breakaway protection (a device that brakes a trailer if it separates from the tow vehicle); fishtailing (side-to-side swaying of a trailer with too little hitch weight); lane position (the part of the lane a motorcyclist chooses in order to see and be seen); placard (the marking that shows a truck's hazardous cargo).

Dynamic facts: the two-thirds crash statistic is a research figure stated only as printed; the trailer thresholds and motorcycle rules are stable content of this printing.

corpus_stability.reason: The Hawaii Driver's Manual is a periodically reprinted reference (imprint HMG 5/2023, copyright line through 2023); the the licensing and responsibilities of large-vehicle drivers, the visibility, space, stopping, acceleration, downgrade and slipstream limitations of large vehicles, hazardous materials and emergency equipment, towing trailers safely, and sharing the road with motorcycles at intersections, in lanes, when following and when passing rules on pages 85–94 are statutory and procedural content that changes less than once a year, so no BlockedProbe.
